title: Who is this one?
hookLine: the Aitareya asks who the self is, twice
carry: the self sees, and is never seen
tomorrow: so is the knowing in me Brahman? two great teachers disagree.
last: NO SINGLE POWER IS THE WHOLE PERSON.

cards: How are you? Fine. Then a friend asks again, slower: no, how are you?
Everyone knows the second time is the real question. The last part of the Aitareya Upanishad opens the same way. Who is this one, the one we honor as the self, the atman?
And at once, again: which one is the self? A question asked twice in a row. That's the odd detail, and it means the quick answer won't do.

teach.h: THE QUICK ANSWER: THE ONE WHO SEES.
teach.b: So what's the quick answer the text is getting past? Probably the one anyone would give: the self is the one who sees, the one who hears. The Aitareya answers by pointing, and the pointing is careful.

teach.h: THAT BY WHICH THE EYE SEES.
teach.b: The self, it says, is that by which one sees form, hears sound, smells scents, speaks words, and tells sweet from not sweet. Not the eye. That by which the eye sees.
Try it with a sound in the room. There's the sound. There's the hearing of it.

And there's something that knows the hearing is going on. The first answer, the one who sees, still treats the self like one more object, a little person sitting behind the eyes. The second asking pushes past that.
The text keeps walking back, from the thing, to the sense, to the knowing, and it never turns the knowing into one more thing to look at.

teach.h: THE KNOWING IS NEVER AN OBJECT.
teach.b: A few lines on, it gives that knowing a name, prajnana, and then the short sentence the tradition lifted out: prajnanam brahma, the knowing is Brahman.
So the puzzle solves itself. The question had to be asked twice because the first answer points at something seen. The second points at whatever is doing the seeing, which is also whoever is asking.

how: In Vedanta study a student hears a great saying explained by a teacher, reflects on it, and returns to it in quiet meditation; the Aitareya's question, who is this one?, is often the starting point for prajnanam brahma.

o: four teachers who wrote the Upanishads down
four questions asked at the start of a lesson
four great sayings that name the self as Brahman

games.q: the question asked twice. tap the pairs.
p: who is this one we honor as the self?
that by which the eye sees

s: the Aitareya says the self is the one who sees
it says the self is that by which one sees: the knowing, not one more seer behind the eyes.
the last part of the Aitareya opens by asking 'who is this one?'
and it asks again at once: which one is the self?
in the passage, the knowing can be looked at, like a sound
the text walks back from thing to sense to knowing, and never makes the knowing an object.

games.q: a friend says: 'i found my true self. it's my taste in music.' what would the Aitareya's second asking say?
o: the taste is real, but the self is what knows the taste.
perfect: whatever you love most is the self.
taste is fake; throw it out to find the self.
games.why: the Aitareya points past every object, even a loved one, to that by which it is known: prajnana, the knowing.

practice: Let one sound come to you: a fan, traffic, your own breath. Notice the sound, then the hearing of it, then the quiet knowing that hearing is happening.
When a thought pulls you away, come back with the text's question, asked silently, twice: who is this one?

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas, and the question under this one: who is this one? Not the eye, but that by which the eye sees.

orig.note: Sanskrit ko 'yam atma: who is this self? The question that opens the Aitareya's last part.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the self sees, and is never seen; the knowing you can't look at because it's doing the looking. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 3.1 (who is this one whom we worship as the self? which is the self? that by which one sees form, hears sound, smells, speaks, and distinguishes sweet from not sweet)
Aitareya Upanishad 3.2–3 (these are names of prajnana; prajnanam brahma)
